A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Continuous Ensemble Weather Forecasting with Diffusion Models. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including the new Appendix E in v2.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendices C–D report original ERA5 forecasting experiments, numerical benchmark results, temporal-continuity analyses, and example forecasts.

after.justification: v2 retains the original forecasting experiments and adds evaluated DYffusion results and variability estimates from repeated ARCI training.

M1.justification: The lead-time conditioning, fixed or autocorrelated noise, ARCI rollout procedure, training objective, and Heun sampler remain unchanged. Algorithms 1–4 differ principally in notation. The newly stated single-head attention detail in Appendix B does not establish an architecture modification.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same 5.625-degree ERA5 weather data, five predicted variables plus derived wind speed, and forecasts through ten days at hourly, six-hourly, and daily resolutions. Evaluation at lead times omitted during training already appears in v1. DYffusion adds a comparator within this existing coverage.

E2.justification: DYffusion changes from a discussed related method in v1 to an evaluated hourly forecasting baseline in v2 Figures 4b and 10. The existing deterministic, Graph-EFM, autoregressive diffusion, and continuous forecasting comparisons remain. AR-24h is retained as a reference rather than removed.

E3.justification: v2 specifies ten ensemble members for hourly evaluation, whereas v1 states a default of fifty without this exception. This revises the reported setting but does not establish that existing experiments were rerun. The new DYffusion protocol uses a 24-hour training horizon, hourly steps, and only the current conditioning state; other models use two states. Dataset splits and metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds an assessment of sensitivity to network initialization through repeated ARCI training, interpreted as evidence of robustness in Section 5.1 and Appendix C. The existing noise-correlation, linear-interpolation, unseen-lead-time, and qualitative forecast analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v1 explicitly reports that computational limits prevented repeated training and error bars. v2 Appendix C reports five retrainings, evaluated with ten ensemble members each, and adds standard deviations for ARCI-24/6h across all six evaluated variables and three metrics at five and ten days. This introduces substantial uncertainty reporting, although comparator uncertainty and significance tests remain absent.

E6.justification: v2 adds DYffusion RMSE, CRPS, and SSR curves for hourly forecasts in Figures 4b and 10. The retained benchmark point estimates in Table 1 and Appendix C are unchanged; for example, ARCI-24/6h z500 CRPS remains 256.7 at five days and 355.2 at ten days. The additions do not demonstrate improved performance of the retained method between versions.

T1.justification: v1 leaves formal continuity analysis to future work. New Appendix E states continuity and local-Lipschitz assumptions and applies a cited ODE theorem to establish fixed-noise trajectory continuity within the solution's existence domain. Stochastic-noise continuity remains future work. Separately, the rewritten integral Equation 2 introduces a sign inconsistency with the differential ODE retained in Appendix B.

C1.justification: The abstract and four introductory contributions retain their original scope. The conclusion adds an explicit superiority claim over DYffusion and identifies the autoregressive comparison as a GenCast reimplementation, qualified by use of the same neural-network architecture. The principal continuous-forecasting contribution is unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 interprets repeated training as demonstrating initialization robustness and removes the previous limitation concerning absent error bars. It more explicitly frames AR-24h as a coarse-resolution reference and asserts applicability to other diffusion or flow-matching frameworks. Limitations concerning spatial scaling, long-horizon correlations, and sampling cost remain.

D1.justification: The code footnote changes from promised availability at publication to stated availability. Appendix B newly specifies single-head attention at 16-by-32 resolution and documents the DYffusion adaptation, including its weighted loss, dropout rate of 0.2, and absence of artificial diffusion steps. Existing optimizer, hardware, and sampling specifications are largely unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 expands the discussion of DYffusion's dropout sensitivity, potential blurring, and lack of guaranteed temporal continuity. It adds references including Diffusion-LAM, Vincent's denoising-score connection, and ODE/Lipschitz literature, while removing CoDiCast. Publication updates to retained works such as GenCast do not constitute new comparison methods.

P1.justification: v2 expands the ODE and autocorrelated-noise explanations, places qualitative results first, and separates hourly forecasting from generalization to unseen lead times. Terminology, author formatting, and publication headers are also revised. Most prose and the overall section organization remain recognizable.

P2.justification: Several central displays are substantially reorganized. Figure 1 is redrawn to distinguish stochastic noise evolution from diffusion sampling; performance panels are combined in Figure 4; Table 1 separates AR-24h reference rows and revises highlighting. The original Appendix Table 6 becomes separate five-day and ten-day tables accommodating uncertainty. Forecast examples are relocated and relabeled rather than added as new cases.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the central method through an evaluated DYffusion comparison, repeated-training uncertainty that addresses an explicit v1 limitation, and a formal argument replacing deferred fixed-noise continuity analysis. These gains outweigh localized shortcomings: DYffusion uses different conditioning inputs, uncertainty covers only ARCI and uses smaller ensembles than the retained point estimates, and rewritten Equation 2 has a sign inconsistency. The improvement concerns evidential support and rigor, rather than higher retained benchmark scores.
